articles.title: Why Israel’s latest assault on Hebron is so significant for the West Bank
articles.summary: Mass expulsions, blockades and expanding settler control in Hebron threaten to devastate the West Bank economy.
articles.body:
Palestinians in Hebron have been subjected to days of Israeli raids and forced displacement in the latest assault on the occupied West Bank city.

Israel has imposed a lockdown on Palestinians and detained at least 47 Palestinians across Hebron since Friday, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

About 2,500 people have been forced out of the city as some Palestinian homes have been converted into military posts and barracks .

The operations followed a shooting attack on Friday that killed two soldiers while the two Palestinian suspects were also killed.

Here is what to know about Israel’s latest assault on Hebron:

Hebron has been subject to severe collective punishment by Israeli forces that has impacted about 900,000 Palestinians.

The military lockdown began immediately after a Friday morning shooting at a military checkpoint in the Farsh al-Hawa area.

After the closure of all entrances to the city, Israeli forces launched a large demolition operation on dozens of Palestinian buildings.

Troops also stormed the Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhood, forcing dozens of families to flee from their homes at night without any belongings. According to Hebron municipality data, the targeted displacement area covers 350 dunams (35 hectares or 86 acres), and nearly 500 Palestinian families have been uprooted.

Hesham al-Sharbati, a human rights researcher, told Al Jazeera that the military’s actions represent “a complete eviction campaign for a Palestinian residential neighbourhood”. He said what is happening is “a form of ethnic cleansing” and the collective punishment of the Palestinian community “amounts to a war crime”.

Moamar Yousef al-Awiwi, a Hebron municipal council member, said the latest Israeli operation in the city comes after a series of measures aimed at displacing the Palestinian population.

“[It] serves as a crime and collective punishment contrary to all international customs and laws,” he told Al Jazeera.

Rights groups have compared the current assault on Hebron to the tactics used during the January 2025 “Iron Wall” operation in the Jenin and Nur Shams refugee camps , which displaced more than 30,000 people and destroyed over half of their residential buildings.

Hebron is an important city for the Palestinian economy, which is in the midst of a severe crisis caused by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and pogroms and raids by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank.

Hebron accounts for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output and 30 percent of exports, but economic activity has been badly affected by recent Israeli restrictions and assaults.

Hebron has the highest concentration of military obstacles in the West Bank with about 40 percent of the 89 main checkpoints in the occupied territory concentrated in the city’s most highly restricted zones.

Economic researcher Ahmed Abu Qamar said the current restrictions on Hebron will be felt widely due to the city’s economic significance for the West Bank.

“Hebron… [is a] first-class industrial city and is considered one of the most important pillars and foundations of the Palestinian economy regarding [its] broad industrial and commercial base,” Abu Qamar told Al Jazeera. “Any restrictions imposed on it or any closures of its outlets or restrictions on freedom of movement … or military operation[s] will put pressure on the entire Palestinian economy in the West Bank.”

Restrictions on trade and business activity in Hebron lead to “a rise in production costs due to the difficulty of supply and logistical disruption” with businesses likely to miss delivery deadlines.

“Ultimately, the halting of facilities or reducing production lines … [means] many economic facilities will be forced to either completely stop working or reduce their working hours to the minimum,” he added.

The daily life of Palestinians in Hebron is also badly affected by the hundreds of Israeli settlers in the Old City.

Under the 1997 Hebron Protocol, Hebron was divided into two sectors: H1, supposedly under Palestinian civil control, and H2, representing 20 percent of the city. The latter was to remain under complete Israeli security control with 7,000 Palestinians living there subject to the strict dictates of the military apparatus.

Israeli authorities have systematically expanded “closed zones” around settlements in the city centre, which are illegal under international law. In early October, Israeli authorities installed three iron gates across a 200-metre (220-yard) stretch of the Old City, further cutting off historical commercial arteries, such as Shuhada Street, where more than 500 shops have been forcibly shuttered over the years.

Over the winter, many Palestinian residents are forced to navigate dangerous, unlit paths through local cemeteries just to bypass military closures and bag searches.

At the epicentre of the H2 zone lies the Ibrahimi Mosque, revered by Muslims and Jews, who refer to it as the Tomb of the Patriarchs. This 14th-century site is part of the Old City, which UNESCO has recognised as a World Heritage Site, and has been subject to numerous assaults by Israeli settlers.

In 1994, an American-Israeli settler opened fire with an automatic assault rifle inside the sanctuary, killing 29 Palestinian worshippers and prompting the Israeli military to permanently partition the holy site and severely restrict Palestinian access to surrounding neighbourhoods.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced the seizure of planning and construction powers over the mosque and the surrounding H2 zone, stripping the Palestinian municipality of its oversight.

In doing so, Smotrich declared he had abolished vital parts of the 1997 Hebron Agreement , marking a dramatic shift that further entrenches the occupation in the city.

articles.title: Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
articles.summary: Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on housing crisis.
articles.body:
Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests.

Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday.

They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.

Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues.

A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests.

Police said the operation was “proportionate” and that the 25 people arrested in Lisbon were later released and are due in court on Monday.

While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday.

“Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said.

Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.

Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.

The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.

The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.

The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents.

There have also been protests in cities including Paris , where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against government economic policies.

articles.title: Zero-Day Option Traders Are Betting Against Big S&P 500 Swings
articles.summary: While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders have increasingly bet that the S&P 500 Index will remain calm.

An analysis of 0DTE options flow from UBS Group AG derivatives strategist Kieran Diamond shows a marked shift toward tactical traders buying calls and selling puts when the market declines, and doing the opposite during rallies. The net effect of what they term a "counter-trend delta bias" is the equivalent of buying low and selling high, which further suppresses swings on the S&P 500.

Zero-day to expiry options have taken on an outsized importance in the daily moves of the equities gauge, with around 66% of the overall volume expiring within a day, according to Garrett DeSimone at OptionMetrics. That's increased the focus on short-term positioning as both retail and institutional traders seek insight on how options flows are influencing the $66 trillion US benchmark index.

"This counter-trend trading pattern seems to be a response to very rangebound markets," said Diamond. "The magnitude of these options flows means that this can start to look self-fulfilling, with options investors helping to limit price moves in either direction."

This intraday tactical shift since 2024 is notable, with larger volumes trading on smaller moves, helping limit S&P 500 realized volatility. The pattern resembles the stabilizing effect of positive gamma, with traders buying into dips and selling into rallies, much like option dealers who are long gamma and similarly buy declines and sell rallies to stay delta-neutral.

The counter-trend trading bias is one factor that has helped contain moves. Another is the long option-dealer gamma regime often seen in the S&P 500, much of which is driven by the prevalence of a big institutional trader selling one-day iron condors — a put spread and a call spread.

RELATED: Popular Zero-Day Trades Curb Stock Rallies: Options Watch

The growth of the 0DTE counter-trend trading flow is now so great that the net effect outweighs the impact from the option dealer re-hedging, according to UBS.

articles.title: After a long, strange trip, this CEO is close to taking a psilocybin pill to market
articles.summary: Compass Pathways is on the cusp of FDA approval for a proprietary version of psilocybin — the active drug in magic mushrooms.
articles.body:
Compass Pathways wants to use psilocybin to help people with treatment-resistant depression.

Its psilocybin pill, COMP360, could finally be coming to market as soon as next year.

For its CEO, Kabir Nath, it's been a long, strange trip to get to this point.

In 2022, Kabir Nath had a cushy executive job at a pharmaceutical firm that developed anti-psychotic medication.

Then he got a call from a scrappy upstart with a patent on a synthetic version of psilocybin — the active ingredient in magic mushrooms. It hoped to use the compound to help those with treatment-resistant depression.

They wanted him to join as CEO. Nath, whose father died by suicide, bit on their second pitch.

"A number of people have said to me in the last couple of years: 'You do realize what a risk that was,'" Nath told Business Insider about eventually jumping ship for what was, and still is, a drug company without FDA approval for its product.

"I was probably the first really senior executive from traditional pharma to make the move to psychedelics," he added. "But, you know, it was the right thing to do."

Nath's personal risk is now magnified as Compass Pathways finishes filing its final forms ahead of what could be FDA approval as soon as next year, and then a public rollout of its psilocybin pill, called COMP360.

Compass has recently added 150 new hires to its payroll, expanded its marketing division, and moved into new office space in Jersey City in the hope it all works out. "The company is growing rapidly," Nath said.

Though a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson attained FDA approval with a version of ketamine for depression patients in 2019, it is by no means guaranteed that Compass, leveraging a more traditional psychedelic, will get the same approval.

Should the FDA deny Compass' bid, investors would rush to dump their shares, likely sending the company into bankruptcy. The Jersey City office, which just received a new lime green paint job, would be untenable.

If you ask Nath, it would also be bad news for 4 million patients with depression in the US, for whom more traditional antidepressants like SSRIs don't work.

"These are people who have been suffering from depression, and nothing's really working," he said.

Like other drug companies — especially those with a single product — Compass' stock has "been on quite the adventure," Nath said, as the company progressed through various human trials.

When markets closed on Friday, the share price hovered around $11, up $5 from last year. In 2020, when the company went public, shares went for $17.

articles.title: How America can bring film and television production home
articles.summary: The newly introduced Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act seeks to implement a federal tax incentive to combat the trend of film and television production moving overseas.
articles.body:
In the classic Western “Shane,” Joey Starrett hears a hard lesson about Rufus Ryker’s ruthless campaign against the homesteaders: “It’s the same old story … and you can’t learn that lesson but once.”

Today, that story is economic and cinematic. And America has learned this lesson more than once: If you take an industry for granted, its jobs, revenue and know-how move overseas and don’t come back.

Film and television production, an export industry with a $9 billion trade surplus , risks following the same script. Forty-five percent of U.S. films and scripted television shows were shot abroad in 2025, up from about one-third three years earlier. That is not just a scene change. It is skilled work, artistry and investment leaving the U.S.

States have responded aggressively. Georgia provides a revealing close-up. It built a robust production hub with incentives of up to 30 percent, attracting billions in spending, building soundstages, and developing a talented workforce. Marvel spent more than $3 billion in Georgia over nearly a decade , including “Black Panther” and two “Avengers” movies. It later shifted much of that work to the United Kingdom, where national incentives changed the math.

Georgia did what it was supposed to do. It built a formidable screen industry. But a state is not a country. States can influence where projects land; they cannot alone ensure those projects stay in the U.S. That is why the newly introduced Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act aims to create a federal tax incentive to work alongside state programs.

A federal film incentive should be simple, targeted and accountable. The proposed legislation offers a 20 percent tax credit for U.S. production labor, including crew wages. The credit could rise to 30 percent for independent productions, projects filming in qualifying rural opportunity zones or federally declared disaster areas, or those returning from overseas. The goal is clear: bring more film and television work home and create lasting American jobs.

A single movie or television shoot can employ hundreds and support scores of small businesses. Nationally, the industry supports more than 2 million jobs and $202 billion in wages , and 93 percent of its nearly 162,000 businesses employ fewer than ten people. Most are working- and middle-class jobs. Camera operators and editors, for example, earn a median of around $75,000 a year . Grips, electricians, drivers, costume designers, tailors, set designers, construction workers, casting directors, animators, producers, production assistants, and office staff keep cameras rolling. When production leaves, those paychecks and purchase orders go with it.

This is a national industry. Almost 40 states offer film incentives. Oklahoma reports an economic impact exceeding $531 million from its program. Kentucky notes nearly $795 million in production expenditures since 2022. Pennsylvania projects its 2025-26 credits to generate $1.1 billion in economic activity across 35 counties. Utah’s rural film incentive has driven more than $200 million in spending since 2022.

Still, even strong state programs can be outbid when other countries offer more competitive packages. Sixty-five countries offer national production incentives . Some, like Canada , Australia and Japan , combine them with regional programs, giving them an even greater advantage. A federal incentive won’t diminish competition among states; it will strengthen their ability to compete globally while rewarding those that innovate most.

Any federal incentive must include commercials. They are a vital economic pillar of the industry. When commercials leave, a dependable source of work and benefits goes with them. Thousands of middle-class professionals depend on them for income as well as health insurance and pension coverage.

Commercial production has hollowed out at home as shoots move overseas , where countries aggressively court and often win the business. That same dynamic can work in America’s favor, allowing communities across the country to compete for that work.

Many states, including Texas , Pennsylvania , Arizona , Ohio , and Nevada , include commercials in their incentive programs because they create well-paying jobs. A federal credit can enhance that approach, making it easier to produce domestically without forcing people to compete globally by accepting lower rates. The bill currently excludes commercials . That needs to change.

The fair question is whether a federal incentive is a sound investment for the taxpayer. To pass that test, the credit should remain tied to verified U.S. employment, with clear accountability measures so taxpayers can see the results.

The industry won’t stand still. Global competition, changing audience habits, and new technologies are rewriting the script. Disruption isn’t necessarily a threat; it can be an opportunity if America strengthens the infrastructure that generations have built and prepares for the next act.

New filmmakers and storytelling formats will emerge from established studios, independent creators, and platforms not yet invented. The question is whether workers, artists and businesses can build that future here.

The next great American story can come from anywhere. Let’s make sure it gets made in America.

James Babbin is a film and audio producer, an actor and a member of the Coalition for American Production .

articles.title: JetBlue and Virgin Voyages' $2,750 kid-free flight-and-cruise package already sold out for March
articles.summary: Many passengers believe airline etiquette has gotten worse, which could be why more are willing to pay up for premium experiences. Is it worth it?
articles.body:
If you've ever been on a flight with a screaming baby or a toddler kicking the back of your seat, you may have wished there was such a thing as a kid-free flight.

And, now JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages are making it a reality — well, at least for one roundtrip flight.

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 reasons why retirees can't afford to waste time

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

It's part of an industry shift toward "premiumization," especially as airlines face tight margins. But is it worth paying up for premium experiences, or is that money better spent (or saved) elsewhere?

Virgin Voyages already operates adults-only cruises, while several hotel brands offer adults-only all-inclusive resorts (or adults-only sections within larger resorts).

The bundled vacation package offered by JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages is called "Do Not Disturb" and includes a kid-free roundtrip flight from New York to Fort Lauderdale.

The flight (operating as a public charter) is bundled into a vacation package that costs $2,750 for two people, which also includes four nights on Virgin Voyages' Brilliant Lady adults-only cruise from Key West to Bimini Beach Club.

Other perks include private ground transfers and VIP port entry, as well as an in-flight toast "to celebrate the start of the kid-free getaway ," according to a Virgin Voyages press release.

"People have wanted this kind of kid-free from takeoff to sail away for a long time, and now it actually exists," Nirmal Saverimuttu, CEO of Virgin Voyages, said in the release. And, while it's the only offering on the table right now, he also said it's "just the start of what we can build."

This isn't a regular offering (at least not yet). Rather, it's a one-time offer that takes place next March — but it's already sold out.

Is a kid-free flight all it's chalked up to be?

Not only can kids on flights be an annoyance, but they might disrupt your plans altogether.

Back in August, a Porter Airlines flight in Canada was canceled after a toddler stood up on their seat as the plane taxied toward the runway. And, despite efforts by the child's parent and cabin crew, the kid wouldn't put a seatbelt on. By the time the parent and child deplaned, it was too late to fly out of the airport, so the entire flight had to be canceled.

articles.title: When will there be a flying car in your garage? Not anytime soon.
articles.summary: People have been wishing for flying cars since the earliest days of flight and automobiles. Does Tesla’s demonstration earlier this month of a “flying” version of its new Roadster mean we’re close?
articles.body: People have been wishing for flying cars since the earliest days of flight and automobiles. Does Tesla’s demonstration earlier this month of a “flying” version of its new Roadster mean we’re close? If you’re looking for a car that can safely travel on roads and highways while also flying significant distances, then no. But if you want a personal flying machine that operates at relatively low altitudes and travels the distance of most car trips, that’s closer to reality. Enter the fast-growing world of electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, known by the somewhat cumbersome acronym of eVTOLs. They can’t travel on highways, and some don’t even have wheels. But many companies have been racing to develop vehicles straight out of science fiction movies and cartoons, with a few already selling aircraft. “The idea of the ‘flying car’ has captured the public imagination for generations, and today that excitement is driving real investment and innovation across the industry,” said Kristina Menton, vice president of flight at Pivotal, one of the companies making eVTOLs. “The appeal is easy to understand. Why spend 90 minutes in traffic when you could spend 20 minutes in the sky?” The eVTOLs are very lightweight compared to traditional cars, with limited carrying capacity, and can generally fly 100 miles at a time at most. They also can’t operate on roads. But even without driving over asphalt, some proponents believe eVTOLs should be considered an automobile in the strictest definition of that word – a vehicle that can transport you from point A to point B. Flying “cars” can appeal to drivers who want to avoid “roads (that are) are problematic and congested,” said Rani Plaut, cofounder and CEO of Air, an Israeli company that plans to build eVTOLs at a facility in Florida. One company that claims to be developing a true flying car is California start-up Alef. CEO Jim Dukhovny said the initial version, which will have a top speed of about 55 mph, was designed to be both an aircraft and a car instead of adapting one or the other. The 254-pound vehicle uses eight propellers inside its body to get airborne but also has four wheels and is designed for driving. The “Model A” can only carry one person that weighs less than the empty vehicle and doesn’t have standard safety equipment like airbags. But Dukhovny wants it to be thought of as a car, not an eVTOL. “EVTOLS are for the aviation market,” he said, “Our competition is Toyota, Ford, Tesla.” But trying to do both, operate as a car and an aircraft, faces many basic engineering problems, said Roger Connor, curator of the vertical flight collection at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum. That’s because aircraft are sensitive to weight, while cars need heavy equipment. “Something that is a hybrid between the two is going to be a poor-performing aircraft and a poor-performing vehicle,” he told CNN. Still, the Federal Aviation Administration has pushed for the development of eVTOLs, launching a series of testing programs across 26 states in March. “The future of aviation is here — and it’s going to dramatically improve how people and products move,” said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy when announcing the program. One thing the FAA is investigating is who will be allowed to fly these aircraft. The expectation is that it will take far less training to fly an eVTOL than to pilot a small plane, helicopter or passenger plane – perhaps as short as a few days. But that is still a work in progress, Connor said. “We haven’t licensed anybody in these new category aircraft yet,” he told CNN. “This is little bit of a new thing for everybody, and it is especially so for the FAA, since the aircraft are not airplanes and they’re not helicopters.” Despite an appetite from the FAA, eVTOLs are still very much in development. Very few have been built and delivered to customers, and those available are very expensive. Larger versions, or “air taxis” that carry a handful of passengers, will cost more than $1 million each, Connor said. Those for personal use will retail for less, but still cost anywhere from $60,000 up to $400,000 for a two-seat aircraft with some endurance and range. “For $60,000, you’re basically getting a fancy drone that could carry 160 pounds or so for maybe 10 minutes,” he added. Tesla has yet to say how much a “flying” version of its Roadster will cost, and no version, flying or grounded, will be for sale until at least 2028. Unlike most eVTOLs, which use propellers, the Roadster utilized compressed air jets to leap over other cars and propel from the top of a ramp six or seven stories high during its product reveal earlier this month. The Roadster also did not fly any appreciable distance, landing short of even the 120 feet the Wright Brothers achieved during their first flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Tesla’s own site cautions the test model is “not approved for public road use.” Still, the splashy demonstration has many in the industry cheering. “When a company with Tesla’s reach puts the idea of everyday people leaving the ground in front of millions of viewers, it widens the conversation, and the industry benefits from that curiosity,” said Pivotal’s Menton. But she cautions that her company is not a car company. “We build aircraft, not flying cars,” she said.

articles.body:

A $10,000 deductible can make a health insurance plan a very different financial proposition when the worst-case scenario isn't a routine doctor's visit but a seven-figure medical emergency.

Billionaire Cost Plus Drugs co-founder Mark Cuban recently questioned whether people considering high-deductible health plans are fully protected when a major claim is denied.

"So I went down the rabbit hole of trying to determine what are the economics for someone, who is currently healthy, to go to a HDHP with a 10k plus deductible," Cuban said on X in October.

Think Your IRA Can Only Hold Stocks And Funds? Think Again. Here's What A Self-Directed IRA Can Actually Invest In.

Warren Buffett once said, "If you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you will work until you die." Here's how you can earn passive income with just $100.

The question that sent him digging was simple.

"The question I asked is 'I don't trust insurance companies," he posted. "What happens if I have a million dollar emergency and they won't pay' All I can say is WTF."

A high-deductible health plan requires the patient to take on more of the initial medical costs before the insurer begins paying a larger share of covered expenses.

That can mean a healthy person faces thousands of dollars in expenses before insurance starts doing much of the heavy lifting.

But Cuban's concern wasn't simply about having a large deductible. He questioned what happens when an insurer denies a major claim altogether.

He said his research led him to independent review organizations, which can review certain disputed insurance decisions.

One company that surfaced was ExamWorks, which Cuban recognized from a previous case involving a patient he was trying to help.

Trending: There's More Than One Way To Put Cash To Work. Some Accredited Investors Are Looking Beyond Savings Accounts.

Cuban questioned whether the review process creates a conflict when companies involved in insurance claim reviews also count major insurers among their customers.

"The biggest customers of the companies that are the final decision makers for insurance carrier denials, are the biggest insurance companies," Cuban wrote.

He also questioned how state insurance commissioners oversee the arrangement.

Cuban's conclusion was a warning for people considering these plans.

"If you are looking at a HDHP, BE CAREFUL. It might just be rigged against you," he wrote.

articles.title: Trump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports
articles.summary: Just as American cattle went to market, Trump’s action added unease to an industry already facing uncertainty.
articles.body:
In late August, United States President Donald Trump announced a 90-day pause on certain beef tariffs, making beef cheaper to import, particularly from Brazil.

That decision was framed as a way to bring down prices for consumers, but it landed as a betrayal for many US ranchers, who were getting ready to take their cattle to market.

It is too soon to tell how the decision will ultimately affect grocery prices, but the impact on ranchers was immediate: prices at cattle auctions plummeted, temporarily lowering ranchers’ profits. The United States Cattlemen’s Association, the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association and the Farm Bureau, all member organisations that represent ranchers, opposed the decision.

Rural Republican members of Congress also distanced themselves, but it is not yet clear how ranchers will vote in the midterms — or whether those votes will decide races.

Chad Basinger, a rancher in Pretty Prairie, Kansas, is sceptical that the imports will have a significant impact.

“I know there’s people that have said, ‘Well I’m just gonna vote for the other party’ or ‘I’m not gonna vote’ or ‘This administration’s really let me down’. So yes, there will be people that swing the other way in the midterms. But overall I don’t think it’ll be that much,” Basinger said.

Ranchers will also be weighing the administration’s other actions, Basinger said, such as the $8bn in farm relief announced in Kansas on October 19.

Basinger’s House of Representatives district in Kansas is expected to remain safely Republican in the midterms. But Kansas faces an unexpectedly tight Senate race and ranchers in House districts elsewhere may find themselves closer to the political fray: potential swing districts in Montana, Iowa, Texas and Colorado are all in cattle country.

Still, it is unlikely that ranchers alone will decide elections: ranchers — along with farmers more broadly — represent a shrinking percentage of rural voters and a smaller voting bloc in practice than in the public imagination.

America’s cattle herd is near its smallest size since 1951 and the number of ranchers has declined alongside the number of livestock. Observers worry that ongoing uncertainty fuelled by tariffs, fuel prices and drought may cause the ranching population to shrink further.

David Anderson, an agricultural economist at Texas A&M University who advises ranchers, said that high prices this year should have given ranchers the confidence to invest in the future and expand their herds. Making imports cheaper, however, may have helped nudge ranchers in the opposite direction.

“It really works against the market signal to expand and produce more domestically,” Anderson said. “That got a lot of people pretty angry.”

This is not the first time that Trump’s tariffs have impacted cattle supplies. Last year, the president added a 50 percent tariff on Brazil, a key trade partner for beef, raising the cost of importing Brazilian lean beef, which is often mixed with fatty US beef to make hamburger patties, a staple in most homes.

In February, Trump allowed more tariff-free beef imports from Argentina. In August, he did the same for Brazil and Paraguay.

Both tariff changes led to swift price swings in cattle futures markets, which are often volatile in response to the news cycle.

Cattle prices also moved this year in response to more fundamental drivers of supply and demand: plant closures by meatpackers, labour shortages late last month related to ICE actions at Kansas packing plants, the second-largest in the country, and the reopening of the southern border after a closure due to New World screwworm disease.

Big picture, the shrinking US cattle herd has less to do with short-term price changes and more to do with drought cycles, which are growing more intense as warming temperatures increase evaporation.

Still, tariff changes add uncertainty. “This has been a hot topic for the last six weeks,” said Anderson. “It just adds a little more uncertainty or volatility — or worries or stress.”

This year, extra price volatility as many ranchers prepared to sell meant ranchers faced lower profits and more risk.

Basinger says that for many established ranchers, the tariff announcement was frustrating, but not existential.

“People are upset. They have a right to be upset. But they’re not going to change their strategy,” he said. For most ranchers, Basinger said, the imports would not be the biggest factor shaping decisions about their herds this year.

Where price volatility may matter more, Basinger said, is for the next generation. Most of today’s ranchers are eyeing retirement. Their heirs must decide whether to make a go of ranching or sell their family’s land. Other aspiring ranchers are also watching the industry.

“If you’re seeing your dad not make money, or somebody else not make money…it’s not easy work!” Basinger said. “It has to be very enticing for somebody to want to jump in and be like, ‘I’m gonna be a rancher and go break ice in the middle of winter when it’s cold and I could be inside’.”

This year, low US cattle supplies meant that ranchers commanded record-high cattle prices, despite added imports and other market shifts.

But high revenue doesn’t always mean huge profits: Many ranchers operate at a loss for years in a row. Then, they rely on a few good years to pay down debts or expand their herds.

This year, profits were lower than hoped, because ranchers also faced high costs.

Interest rates on loans are high and the war with Iran meant ranchers paid extra for fuel and fertiliser. A drought across much of America’s ranchland meant they paid more for feed.

In states such as Kansas and Nebraska, ranchers also faced destructive wildfires and aid groups like Farm Rescue coordinated hay donations.

Still, Basinger said, ranchers who raise cows and calves generally did well this year. In Kansas, he is seeing ranchers use profits to make repairs and upgrades. He said this year’s high cattle prices have been helping. “But it needs to help for a little longer to give them more of an edge,” he said.

More of an edge might mean, for example, enough money for bigger purchases, like buying land from a neighbouring ranch to make room for a growing herd.

Rangeland, however, is increasingly expensive. When it is up for sale, outside investors can often pay more than ranchers, which can mean less land for cattle. That’s just one more pressure shrinking the US herd decade after decade.

Ranchers had hoped that 2026 would be a turnaround year. So far, however, “we really don’t have much evidence of herd expansion,” Anderson said.

articles.title: What Boomer Parents Spent To Raise a Child vs. What Parents Spend Today
articles.summary: Let's explore the details between how much boomer parents spent to raise a child versus how much it costs parents today.
articles.body:
Ask a boomer what groceries or babysitting cost when their children were small and the answer may sound almost fictional.

A $65,250 price tag for raising a child sounds almost quaint now, yet that was the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) figure — as reported by the Washington Post — that made headlines in 1980, right in the thick of peak boomer parenthood.

In 1995, when baby boomers were roughly 31 to 49 years old, a middle-income family would spend about $137,000 in the urban Midwest (or $157,000 in the urban West) to raise a child, per the USDA . While, the latest widely-cited estimate for raising a child today is $320,661, according to Northwestern Mutual .

Let's explore the details between how much boomer parents spent to raise a child versus how much it costs parents today .

What Did Raising a Child Cost Around 1980?

One important point that complicates this whole issue is that these estimates are expressed in 1978 dollars.

The 1980 Washington Post article explained that the USDA based its work on spending reported by 20,000 to 30,000 families in the 1973 Consumer Expenditure Survey. UPI reported the estimate as $65,250 through age 18, excluding college, which also fails to account for inflation.

Using the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis CPI (Consumer Price Index) series, $65,250 in 1978 had roughly the buying power of $322,000 in 2025.

What Was Missing From the Boomer-Era Number?

The 1980 calculation left out day care and the value of a mother's time. The survey didn't break down those costs because two-earner households weren't yet seen as a major problem when the data was collected.

That's a huge omission by modern standards. According to the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), median annual child care prices for one child ranged from $5,357 to $17,171 in 2022 dollars (depending on the child's age, care setting and county size). That eats up 8% to 19.3% of median family income for families buying care, according to the DOL .

But boomer households were already in the midst of change. The share of mothers with children under age 18 who were also working or looking for work rose from 47.4% in 1975 to 56.6% in 1980, per the DOL . According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), it had reached 73.9% by 2025 and more working parents meant more families had to solve the care problem with money or help from relatives.

articles.title: 'The world's super company': Wall Street weighs SpaceX earnings, company's likely Tesla tie-up
articles.summary: Wall Street is starting to size up the potential of a combined SpaceX and Tesla.
articles.body:
Elon Musk's vision for SpaceX ( SPCX ) has Wall Street sizing up a potential giant unlike anything it's seen before. Mix in a possible tie-up with Musk's EV giant Tesla ( TSLA ), and investors could be looking at a monster play.

Wall Street strategists are already looking at SpaceX and Tesla as one.

Musk, who is CEO of both companies, projects SpaceX's annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 to fall "somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion." Its booming AI compute business is fueling bets that SpaceX could emerge as a fifth hyperscaler alongside Meta ( META ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).

"Couple that with the fact that they have a satellite business that's growing, they have a lucrative space business that the AI profits can continue to underwrite, and now we have a possible merger with Tesla," Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told Yahoo Finance after the space company posted better-than-expected quarterly results.

"This doesn't only become the fifth hyperscaler, this becomes the world's super company," he added.

A deal with Tesla would bring SpaceX into the EV maker's plans to roll out Optimus robots, its Cybercab business, and ultimately Terafab, Musk's ambitious plan to manufacture chips and reduce production costs by up to 90%.

"This is their way of bypassing Nvidia and bypassing TSMC," RBC Capital Markets lead equity analyst Tom Narayan told Yahoo Finance. "If they can do that, it's huge."

Those chips would power everything from data centers to hundreds of thousands of humanoid robots. Tesla plans to produce 20,000 Optimus per week by the end of 2027.

Canaccord Genuity Capital Markets analyst George Gianarikas raised his price target on Tesla to $442.00 from $410 following the EV maker's quarterly results, with the call based fundamentally on a merger.

"If they merge, you are buying the future of the physical world," wrote Gianarikas on Thursday. "A company that is attempting to make, not just program, Tomorrowland. You are buying the Berkshire Hathaway of tomorrow's physical technology."

Meanwhile, JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth more than doubled his price target on SpaceX to $500 after the company posted better-than-expected quarterly results last week. On Friday, shares were trading at $146.

SpaceX has grown well beyond rockets and satellites with plans to become a leading mobile carrier and build out data centers in space.

"SpaceX's ambitions are bigger than any company's we've seen — to make life multi-planetary, leverage the Sun to build out AI in space, & build bases on the Moon and cities on other planets, " wrote Anmuth.

articles.title: Banks pass on rate hikes, but go slow when rates fall
articles.summary: MUMBAI: A study by RBI has found that interest rates adjust upward more completely during a tightening phase than they do downward during an easing phase.
articles.body: MUMBAI: A study by RBI has found that interest rates adjust upward more completely during a tightening phase than they do downward during an easing phase.According to the study, published in RBI Bulletin, banks passed on 76.4% of the repo rate increase through contract repricing, with lending rates rising by 191 basis points following a 250-basis-point hike between March 2022 and Jan 2025.During the easing phase between Feb 2025 and March 2026, they passed on only 64% of the rate reduction, with lending rates falling by 80 basis points following a 125-basis-point cut. The study, titled ‘Transmission to Lending Rates of SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects in WALR’, notes that changes in the weighted average lending rate (WALR) reflect both changes in lending rates and shifts in loan-book composition.While monetary policy pass-through to contracted loan rates was notably lower during the easing cycle (64%) than in the tightening cycle (76.4%), this gap narrowed significantly when evaluating the headline WALR—which captures shifts in credit composition—narrowing the pass-through disparity to 74.4% in the easing phase compared to 72.4% during tightening. During tightening, the 250-basis-point hike resulted in a 181-basis-point increase in WALR, and during easing, the 125 bps cut resulted in a 93 bps decline in the average rate.During easing cycles, banks protect net interest margins (NIMs) by raising spreads or shifting towards higher-yielding loans, weakening rate-cut transmission. In March 2026, fresh lending rates rose 12 basis points despite the easing stance, according to RBI researchers Yuvraj Kashyap, Kamal Gupta and Arvind Jha.MSME loans had the biggest impact on fresh-loan WALR, with rates falling 122 basis points during the Feb 2025-March 2026 easing cycle, against a 125-basis-point repo cut. For MSMEs, benchmark-linked repricing accounted for 118 basis points, reducing system-wide WALR by 24 basis points, over 2.6 times any other sector’s contribution.Education loan rates fell the most, by 162 basis points, but contributed virtually nothing to the overall WALR decline because of their small share of credit. Rupee export credit rates fell 161 basis points but contributed just five basis points. articles.summary: MUMBAI: Information technology has become a core function of RBI, with secure, sovereign data centres and cybersecurity capabilities increasingly critical
articles.body: MUMBAI: Information technology has become a core function of RBI, with secure, sovereign data centres and cybersecurity capabilities increasingly critical to the resilience of the financial system as AI transforms technology, governor Sanjay Malhotra said.In an interview with Doordarshan following the inauguration of RBI’s new data centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Malhotra said the central bank needed to strengthen its technological infrastructure while keeping pace with emerging technologies.“IT no longer is a support function. It is a very core function because it is from where all our applications for the general public, for our own use, and for consumers run,” he said.The data centre will host applications supporting critical payment systems (NEFT & RTGS), govt banking operations and services for consumers of regulated financial entities. While the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) operates the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), settlement ultimately takes place through the data centres and applications built by RBI, Malhotra said.The sovereign data centre, with four independent facilities and Tier IV accreditation, will improve efficiency, uptime and resilience. RBI has also applied for a platinum green-building rating, using local materials to blend with the surroundings. Two-thirds of the Bhubaneswar site houses a cybersecurity training institute, reflecting AI-driven security risks.Inaugurating the facility, PM Modi stressed secure digital infrastructure and technological self-reliance. Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said it would house critical systems, including RTGS/NEFT, while building expertise in cybersecurity and emerging technologies. This will have an impact on exports as well as the entire supply chain when container shortages are seen in the eastern hemisphere, along with port congestion in certain parts of the world.On Oct 22, the Drewry World Container Index was at $4,585 for a 40-feet container, compared with $1,746 on Oct 25, 2025.“It is already pushing freight rates beyond a point. Right now, buyers are managing because they were short of inventory. Now, that they are stocked up, it is unclear if they can absorb higher freight. Fresh disruption in West Asia will have an adverse impact for rest of the world too,” said Ajai Sahay, director general at Fieo. He said container rates to West Asian ports have shot up from $800 to $8,000 to $10,000 now.“The East-West container freight market remains uncertain. Security risks and attacks on ships continue to affect vessel movements through the Gulf, with only two containerships sailing into the Gulf in Week 42, down from five the previous week. Meanwhile, sailings through the Suez Canal increased slightly, from 54 in Week 41 to 55 in Week 42,” Drewry said.There are also concerns over crew and vessels entering the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as the epicentre of the conflict. In any case, most businesses reckon that any uncertainty, especially a war that has implications on global energy supplies, is best avoided.Oil is the biggest concern with crude price for Indian refiners averaging $120 a barrel in Oct, the highest monthly average in 12 years. And, with petrol averaging $140 a barrel and diesel at over $154, the pressure on state-run retailers in mounting as they incur losses, given that pump prices are linked to the import price of the product.Although govt had shielded them through duty cuts and permission to raise prices subsequently, the Centre has limited headroom for fiscal concessions. Already, fuel and fertiliser subsidies are well past last year’s level and it will have to provide extra, if the need arises.For the moment, top officials said, fertiliser companies took advantage of a falling price window to stock up for the next season and the fertiliser ministry had some surplus cash with it due to the savings.There is some cushion for the Centre due to higher-than-budgeted disinvestment receipts and dividends from state-run financial institutions and RBI, with tax collections holding up so far, which is expected to keep the fiscal deficit within the target of 4.3% of GDP. But, a spike in the import bill due to higher commodity prices will have impact on the trade deficit and the current account deficit. articles.title: Dalal Street braces for volatile week
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Rising geopolitical risks, elevated crude oil prices, a weakening rupee and unabated foreign fund selling have combined to force Dalal Street
articles.body: MUMBAI: Rising geopolitical risks, elevated crude oil prices, a weakening rupee and unabated foreign fund selling have combined to force Dalal Street investors on the back foot. As a result, markets are bracing for another volatile week. In addition to the above factors weighing on sentiment, there are talks of renewed military attacks on Iran by the US-Israel combine ahead of the crucial polls in the two countries where the incumbent heads of state are expected to face severe election setbacks.One of the highlights of the week would be the listing of Jio Platforms which on Friday closed the biggest IPO in India ever and is expected to list on Oct 28.As talks of an escalation in war in the Persian Gulf circulated, Brent crude prices jumped to above the $114 per barrel level on Friday and settled at about the $112 level, levels not seen since May this year. That also weakened the rupee which again inched closer to the 95-to-a-dollar level at close on Friday. The only positive for the week was that foreign funds were net buyers in two of the five sessions.During the week, foreign funds significantly reduced their selling and even turned buyers on two days, said VK Vijayakumar, the chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments. “The moderation in the US bond yields with the 10-year yield declining from 5.36% to around 5%, appreciation in the rupee to 94.94 to the dollar and the low valuations, particularly of the large-caps, contributed to the moderation in FII selling,” he said.Vijayakumar, however, pointed out that in Oct, net selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in stocks was Rs 53,337 crore while the corresponding figure for the year so far was Rs 3.7 lakh crore (excluding IPO proceeds), the highest ever yearly figure.Friday’s session also saw a sharp slide in midcap and smallcap stocks. And this could be due to forced liquidation in the margin-funded long positions in the market. For long, several of the top market players have been warning about the growing size of the margin trade funding (MTF) book that has doubled in the last two years to about Rs 1.5 lakh crore now.During midweek, Jio Platforms, after its hugely successful IPO of Rs 30,213 crore was subscribed over 22 times, will list on the bourses.
